newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - Thin but steady week forseen.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - Thin but steady week forseen.

text.p: European crude values are pinned between poor refining margins dampening demand and absent Iraqi barrels still tightening supply, traders say.

With neither factor likely to change dramatically this week crude differentials should largely hold steady, while outright Brent values will move in the $18-$19 range in a recovery from the pre-U.S. holiday weekend sell-off.
"The most important thing on everyone's mind is still Iraq," said one crude trader who buys both in Europe and the Mediterranean.
"I think this week we'll be closer to a breakthrough on Iraq and I think we'll see barrels from them at the beginning of August, just like everyone predicts."

Crude differentials jumped last week, pushing July Brent into backwardation against further forward months, after Baghdad said it was unlikely to resume exports under the second term of its U.N. oil-for-food deal until August.
Crude buyers snapped up non-Brent North Sea cargoes, leaving very few available from the July loading programme, and front month Brent futures gained $1 before Thursday.

But when Baghdad said it was ready to present the aid distribution plan it needed to prepare before the $2.14 billion oil sales programme could start, it was a cue for futures players to liquidate long positions.
August Brent contracts lost 70 cents on Thursday and front month WTI slumped by 78 cents a barrel.
"I think 70 cents was too strong, it was just the U.S. closing positions before Independence Day," said one broker.
"They didn't want to come back from their barbecues to huge losses. I think we'll quickly be back to $18.50."
The Security Council agreed on June 8 to roll over the deal to let Iraq sell crude to pay for war reparations, arms monitoring costs, food and medicines.
But disputes over the U.N.'s slow approval of aid contracts from the first oil-for-food deal delayed the resumption of crude exports.
The prolonged absence of Iraqi barrels has forced buyers to scramble for alternatives and the resulting price increases hammered the profits of refinery operators.
Less complex processing units running Brent in northern Europe and Russian Urals in the Mediterranean were making losses last week, with operators talking gloomily about imminent run cuts.
Thursday's price fall brought some relief but Med hydroskimmers were still losing some 30 cents a barrel.

With most July end-user commitments already met, buyers would use poor margins as an excuse not to buy barrels, forcing sellers of what little remains to let differentials slip, some traders predicted.
"There are not many buyers looking for crude," said a sour market trader in the Med. "I don't see the market falling too far but it has definitely peaked."
He saw Urals holding in a range of Dated Brent -70 to -80 cents, after trading at a high of -65 cents last week.
